title: Shadows of Malice - A Video with Some Thoughts
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HvQpYQlLGzg

Daniel (@dungeondive) opens with a thank-you to his first Patreon supporters, then finally sets up a game he had owned for a long time without playing: Shadows of Malice, Jim Felli's co-op epic fantasy from Devious Weasel Games. He admits it never excited him. The premise is grand, but the box looks plain and the rulebook reads like a technical manual. Then he read the designer's note. The game was meant to have no art at all, and the rough placeholder sketches on the treasure cards survived only because every playtest group asked to keep them.

That minimalism turns out to be the whole point. Your avatars of light are coloured tokens, so you have to imagine them. His pathfinder becomes a hawk-faced tribesman, his blood singer a body of congealed blood wrapped like a mummy. Monsters are rolled up on the spot from terrain, nature and power, plus a drawn ability such as a displacer-beast shimmer. Daniel says this succeeds where City of Kings failed him: here nothing contradicts a written backstory, because there isn't one.

You set the length by choosing how many map tiles to use, at about ninety minutes each. He praises the rulebook's "prepare, buff and reveal" guide to the three stages of play, but thinks it belongs on the first page,. This is first impressions, not a review, and his verdict is that it's a crunchy, imaginative outlier that takes a few plays to click.

----

Shadows of Malice gives you coloured tokens instead of hero art. Does a game that makes you imagine its world draw you in, or leave you cold?
